data.summary: Investigate further. The strategy is the Jegadeesh-Titman decile momentum rule: rank stocks on their past six-month return and hold the winners for six months, here long-only on a 415-name S&P 500 survivor universe over 2015-2025. The long-only portfolio earned a net CAGR of 14.54% against 12.71% for the equal-weighted universe, with a Sharpe of 0.68 against 0.65, but robustness is weak. The edge fails at 10 bps, holds in 0 of 2 sub-periods, and the group rho of -0.28 runs opposite to the expected momentum ordering. The simulated fund economics are positive, with P(NPV > 0) of 76% and a median incremental fee PV of $2.0M against the equal-weighted fund, but this rests on an assumed fee schedule. Performance and economics argue for continuing, while the weak robustness and the missing winner-minus-loser spread stop short of a pursue call.

sections.paper_proposes: Jegadeesh and Titman (1999) test whether momentum profits survive alternative explanations. The experiment we selected is Table 1: each month, NYSE/AMEX stocks are ranked on their past six-month return (months -5 to 0) and sorted into ten equal-weighted decile portfolios. Each portfolio is held for six months with no skip period, using overlapping monthly cohorts. Stocks priced below $5 are excluded. The paper reports a winner-minus-loser spread of 1.11% per month in 1965-1989 (t=4.61), 1.01% per month in 1990-1997, and 1.09% per month in 1965-1997 (t=5.65). It attributes the profits to underreaction or delayed overreaction to information.
sections.implemented_and_changed: We implemented the signal as a six-month cumulative return with no skip, ten equal-count groups, equal weights, a six-month hold with monthly rebalancing, and 10 bps of trading cost. Five fields were adapted. The universe is 415 names from today's S&P 500 constituents, eligible from their index add date, with 19 names excluded for missing data. Breakpoints are equal-count over eligible names rather than exchange-based. The strategy is long-only in the favored group, with every group still computed for a monotonicity check. The sample is 2015-01-01 to 2025-12-31, with a warm-up from 2012-01-01. The $5 price floor was not applied because the snapshot's prices are split-adjusted rather than as-traded, so a dollar floor would drop the wrong names. Two defaults were assumed because the paper is silent: one year of history to be eligible, and at least 15 trading days in a formation month. The extraction also left 15 details unresolved, including return convention, delisting treatment, share-code filters and NYSE-only breakpoints, so engine defaults apply to those.
sections.backtest_found: Net of costs the strategy returned a CAGR of 14.54% against 12.71% for the equal-weighted universe and 13.45% for SPY by the engine's own figures (0.134530). Net Sharpe was 0.68 against 0.65 for the equal-weighted universe and 0.686041 for SPY. Maximum drawdown was -0.342222. The monthly excess over the equal-weighted universe has a Newey-West t of 1.09607, and over SPY 0.767553, so neither is statistically distinguishable from zero. The four-factor alpha t is 0.32. The momentum factor loading is 0.328854 with a t of 10.8912, so much of the return is explained by known factor exposure. The spanning alpha t is -0.170382. Alpha t is 0.548033 at 0 bps and -0.020555 at 25 bps. The paper's key pattern does not appear in the groups. The favored group's mean monthly return is only marginally different from the loser group's (-0.000199, Newey-West t -0.06847), and the Spearman rho across groups is -0.28 (p 0.425038), opposite to the expected direction. Both sub-periods show a CAGR close to the full-sample figure, but neither passes the robustness test.
sections.simulation_and_economics: The simulation bootstraps historical days in 126-day average blocks for 1000 paths over a 5-year horizon. It models a $100M long-only fund charging 2/20 with a 5% hard hurdle and a high-water mark, a schedule that is an assumption rather than an observed fee. Incremental fees are measured against an equal-weighted universe fund charged the same fees. P(NPV > 0) is 76% and the median incremental fee PV is $2.0M. When the historical mean excess return over the equal-weighted fund is removed, the NPV-positive share falls to 0.477. That is consistent with the positive result depending on the historical excess return rather than on structure alone. The strategy beats the equal-weighted fund in 0.763 of paths but beats SPY in only 0.111. Block-length sensitivity gives 0.723333, 0.766667 and 0.793333 for 63, 126 and 252 days. Mean monthly turnover is 0.151131. Trading costs are 0.003664 of average value per year. The largest single-trade participation is 0.072465 of average daily volume, and no trades exceed 10% of it. Break-even AUM is 900181.0, which is well below the $100M starting AUM.
sections.interpretation_reliability: The engine rates implementation reliability green. Evidence was valid for 100% of the 16 checked fields, there were no critical check disagreements, and 2 fields were assumed. The three extraction runs agreed on average at 0.851852 across fields, but agreement was only 0.333333 on the economic rationale, the breakpoints and the selected experiment. Scoring against the reference interpretation is weaker: the agreement rate is 0.357143, with critical errors flagged on the signal formula wording and the favored group. That reference is explicitly preliminary. It labels P1 as losers, the opposite of the paper's quote, so the flagged items look like labeling differences, but they have not been resolved. The result also carries structural limitations: a survivor universe that omits delisted names and flatters returns, a post-publication sample, long-only equal weighting, zero cash yield, Yahoo adjusted-close conventions, and an assumed fee schedule.
sections.next_steps: First, resolve the favored-group labeling disagreement with a corrected reference. Second, test whether the absent winner-minus-loser spread is an artifact of the 415-name large-cap survivor universe. Rerun on a broader universe that includes delisted names and has as-traded prices so the $5 floor can be applied. Third, add the short leg, or at least a long-short comparison, since the paper's claim concerns the spread, not the long side alone. Fourth, check whether the long-only result is mostly momentum factor exposure, given the loading and the spanning result. Finally, treat the economics as provisional until a fee schedule from a real vehicle replaces the assumed 2/20 structure.
